q: A team only has browser tests that click through checkout. The suite takes 40 minutes, and a failure just says the total is wrong. What would unit tests for the pricing code mainly add?
options: Fast runs, and failures that point at the exact function that broke
More realism, since they run the whole app the way a user would
Checks that the checkout page layout renders correctly in each browser
A full replacement for the browser tests, which can then be deleted
why: A unit test runs a small piece of logic in isolation, in milliseconds. When it fails, its name and input point to the function that broke, so you find the bug without tracing through the whole app.
wrong: That describes end-to-end tests. Unit tests trade realism for speed and precise failures.
Unit tests of pricing logic never render a page; layout needs UI-level tests.
Unit tests cannot see how the pieces fit together, so a few end-to-end tests are still worth keeping.

q: Unit tests for a UserRepository pass with a mocked database, but in production its SQL query names a column that does not exist. Which test would have caught this?
options: Another unit test, with a mock that returns a realistic sample user row
An integration test that runs the query on a real test database
Only a full end-to-end test that goes through the web UI
Raising the line coverage of UserRepository to 100%
why: The bug sits between the code and the database, and the mock never reads the SQL text. An integration test runs the real query against a real test database, so the missing column fails at once.
wrong: The mock returns whatever it was told to, so the wrong column name is never checked.
An end-to-end test could catch it too, but slower and with a vaguer failure; an integration test is enough.
The lines already ran, but against the mock, so running them proved nothing about the SQL.

q: Your team wants to write most tests as end-to-end tests, since they are the most realistic. Why do most teams keep end-to-end tests few and focused on key user flows?
options: They are less realistic than unit tests, because they run against test servers
They cannot find real bugs, since real users never follow scripted paths
They are slow, flaky and hard to debug, so many cost more than they catch
They check exactly the same things as unit tests, so they add nothing new
why: An end-to-end test starts the whole system, so it is slow, depends on many moving parts and can fail for reasons unrelated to the change. Its failure also says little about where the bug is. A few cover key flows; faster tests cover the details.
wrong: They are the most realistic kind; their cost is speed and stability, not realism.
They do catch real bugs, especially in how the parts are wired together; that is why a few are kept.
They catch wiring and configuration bugs that unit tests cannot see.

q: All unit and integration tests pass, but users cannot log in: the frontend still calls an old API path that the backend removed. Which test would have caught this?
options: A unit test of the login form that uses a mocked HTTP client
An integration test of the backend login handler with its database
A unit test that checks the backend's route table contains the new path
An end-to-end test that logs in through the real UI and backend
why: The bug is in how two deployed parts talk to each other. Only a test that runs the real frontend against the real backend sends the actual request to the actual path, so it fails when the two disagree.
wrong: The mocked client answers any path, so the test passes with the old URL.
The backend works on its own; this test never involves the frontend that sends the wrong path.
The new route does exist; the problem is that the frontend does not use it.

q: A function suggests an umbrella when the weather API says rain. The test must not call the real API, and it does not care how the API is called. What should stand in for the API?
options: A stub that always returns rain
A mock that fails unless it is called exactly once with the city name
The real API, so that the test stays realistic
A random weather generator, so that many cases get tested
why: The test only needs a fixed answer so the code under test can run. A stub gives that canned answer, and the test then checks the result: an umbrella is suggested.
wrong: Checking the exact call adds an expectation this test does not need, and it breaks when call details change.
A real network call is slow and its answer changes, so the test would not be repeatable.
Random answers change the outcome from run to run; the test can no longer state what it expects.

q: After a successful signup, the code must send exactly one welcome email. The email sender returns nothing. How can a unit test check this?
options: Stub the sender to return success, and assert that signup returns True
Use a mock sender and verify one call with the user's address
Send a real email and have the test read a test inbox
Skip it, since a call with no return value cannot be tested
why: The behavior to check is the call itself, and nothing comes back to assert on. A mock records the calls it receives, so the test can verify the email was sent once, to the right address.
wrong: A stub only feeds answers in; signup could return True without ever sending the email.
That makes a unit test depend on a mail server and the network: slow and flaky.
Side effects are tested by checking the interaction, which is exactly what a mock is for.

q: Many service tests save users and then look them up. Mocking every save and find call made the tests long, and they break on each refactor. Which double fits better?
options: A stub whose find method always returns the same fixed user
The shared staging database that every test run writes to
A fake: an in-memory repository that really stores users
Stricter mocks that also check the order of every call
why: A fake is a small working implementation. Tests save a user, find it and check the result without scripting each call, so they survive refactors that keep the behavior the same.
wrong: A fixed answer cannot show that the user you saved is the one you get back.
A shared database is slow, and runs that write to it at the same time interfere with each other.
Checking more calls ties the tests even closer to the code's internals, so they break more often.

q: The real payment API returns {"state": "paid"}, so in production is_paid raises KeyError. Why did this test pass?
options: Any Mock object is truthy, so the assert passes whatever is_paid returns
The mocking library has a bug; another library would have failed the test
The test tries only one order id; trying more ids would expose the bug
The mock repeats a wrong belief about the API, and nothing checks it
why: A mock returns whatever its author believed the dependency returns. If that belief is wrong, the code and the test agree with each other and are both wrong. Only a test against the real API, or its sandbox, checks the belief.
wrong: is_paid returns the result of ==, a real bool, so the assert does check the value.
The library did exactly what it was told; the wrong data came from the test author.
Every id gets the same mocked response, so more ids repeat the same wrong assumption.

q: A test named test_cart adds items, removes one, applies a coupon and checks the tax, with 14 asserts. It fails at the third assert. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The failure hides which behavior broke, and the later asserts never run
The 14 asserts should go into a loop so the test is shorter
Nothing: more asserts in one test means more thorough testing
It should print the cart after every step so the log is easier to follow
why: One test per behavior, with a clear name, tells you what broke from the name alone. In a combined test the first failing assert stops the test, so the later checks tell you nothing about the code.
wrong: Logic in tests makes them harder to read and makes failures even harder to trace.
Thoroughness comes from covering behaviors, not from piling asserts into one test.
Printing helps read the log, but the test still mixes four behaviors and stops at the first failure.

q: can_vote(age) should return True for 18 and older. If you could test only two inputs, which pair is most likely to catch a bug?
options: 5 and 30, one typical value on each side of the rule
17 and 18, the values on each side of the boundary
30 and 60, two clear adult cases
0 and 120, the smallest and largest possible ages
why: Bugs gather at boundaries: writing > instead of >= breaks only age 18. Testing the last value that should fail and the first that should pass catches that off-by-one, while values far from 18 pass either way.
wrong: Values far from 18 give the same result with > and >=, so they miss the most common bug.
Both are on the same side of the rule, so the False case is never tested.
Extremes are worth testing, but they are far from 18 and miss an off-by-one there.

q: A teammate changed a class to store tags in a set instead of a list. Its public methods behave exactly as before, yet 12 tests fail because they read the private field. What does this show?
options: The refactor broke the class and should be reverted
This is normal: every refactor should require rewriting the tests
The tests check internals, not behavior through the public methods
The private field should be made public so that the tests stay stable
why: Good tests use a class the way callers do. Then a refactor that keeps behavior keeps the tests green, and a failing test means behavior really changed. Tests tied to internals fail on harmless changes and teach the team to ignore failures.
wrong: The public behavior is unchanged, so nothing a caller sees is broken.
Tests are the safety net for refactoring; if every refactor breaks them, they cannot play that role.
Exposing internals for tests spreads the same coupling to production callers.

q: This test passes. Which extra input is most likely to expose a bug in average?
why: An empty list makes len(nums) zero, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError. Empty input, a single element and boundary values are where code most often breaks, so each deserves its own test.
wrong: Another typical list follows the same path as the passing test.
Python integers do not overflow, so large values work fine here.
One element divides by 1 and returns 7.0, which is correct.

q: This test passes on laptops but fails now and then on the busy CI server. What is the best fix?
code:
import time

def test_report_is_generated():
    start_report_job()  # runs in the background
    time.sleep(2)
    assert report_exists()
options: Poll until the report exists, with a time limit
Raise the sleep to 10 seconds to leave more margin
Mark the test to rerun automatically until it passes
Remove the assert so the test only checks that nothing crashes
why: A fixed sleep guesses how long the job takes, and on a slow machine the guess is wrong. Waiting for the actual condition ends as soon as the report is ready, and fails clearly only if it never appears.
wrong: A longer sleep slows every run and can still be too short on a slower day.
Reruns hide the problem and teach the team to treat real failures as noise.
A test that cannot fail no longer checks that the report was made.

q: Each test passes when run alone. When both run, in this order, test_add_two_items fails. Why?
code:
cart = []

def test_add_item():
    cart.append("apple")
    assert len(cart) == 1

def test_add_two_items():
    cart.append("pear")
    cart.append("plum")
    assert len(cart) == 2
options: The runner runs the tests in parallel threads, which corrupts the list
Both tests share the module-level cart, so state leaks between them
len() is unreliable on a list that another function appended to
The second test should assert len(cart) == 3, the correct total
why: cart is created once and shared. After the first test it already holds one item, so the second test sees 3. Each test should build its own fresh state, so the result does not depend on which tests ran before.
wrong: These tests run one after the other; the leak comes from shared state, not threads.
len() is always exact; the list really holds three items.
That makes the second test depend on the first, so it fails when run alone or in another order.

q: A test creates a token that expires in 1 second, then asserts is_expired(token) is False. is_expired reads the system clock. On slow CI runs the test sometimes fails. What makes it deterministic?
options: Give the test token a longer lifetime, such as one hour
Run the test twice and count it as passed if either run passes
Pass the current time in as a parameter, so the test sets it
Read the clock twice inside is_expired and use the later value
why: When time comes in as a parameter or an injected clock, the test fixes it to known values. The result no longer depends on machine speed, and edge cases such as expiring exactly now become easy to test.
wrong: A bigger margin makes failures rarer, but the result still depends on the real clock, and cases like expiring exactly now stay hard to test.
Passing on either run hides the flake instead of removing its cause.
Reading the real clock again still ties the outcome to how fast the machine is.
